Macro history · United States and euro area

After the oil price fell

Does cheaper oil lift industrial output? In December 2014, Brent averaged $62.34 a barrel, down from $111.80 six months earlier. Over the next year US industrial production fell 4.5% and euro-area production rose 1.6%. Both economies had near-zero benchmark policy rates.

The screen starts in January 2000. It selects the first month that Brent’s monthly average falls by the chosen percentage or more over six months. A fresh crossing must occur more than twelve months after the preceding retained event. The crossing month is the baseline for subsequent changes.

Why the two near-zero episodes differed

Cheaper oil reduces costs for firms that use it and reduces revenues for firms that produce it. A fall in demand can also pull oil prices and factory output down together. The Brent price alone cannot separate these channels. Comparing energy prices, core inflation and industrial output in the two economies shows which outcomes moved together after each decline.

In the 30% sample, Brent was still 66.0% below its June 2014 level by December 2015. US core inflation edged up about 0.5 percentage points and euro-area core inflation rose 0.2 points. The US decline in industrial output coexisted with an expansion in the euro area. EIA’s December 2014 assessment identified rising US oil supply, weaker expected demand and OPEC’s decision to maintain its production target. Dollar depreciation or appreciation against the euro also alters the price paid by euro-area importers. EIA December 2014 outlook · ECB December bulletin, indirect effects of oil prices

By March 2021 Brent had exceeded its September 2019 price by 4.1%. Industrial output rose 1.0% in the US and 14.4% in the euro area from March 2020. From September 2019 to the March 2020 crossing, US production had already fallen 4.8% and euro-area production 12.0%. Use the six months before zero on the chart to see how choosing March as the starting point affects the comparison. The rebound cannot distinguish restored supply from the reopening of demand.

Definitions, coverage and sources

The Brent measure is EIA’s monthly Europe spot price, free on board, in US dollars per barrel. All observations were available by 20 November 2026. Macro series incorporate revisions. The reference price is the observed price six months before the crossing. Changing the threshold can change both the sample and the month used as zero. US and euro-area observations on one global price fall share the same event.

Industrial production measures real output, seasonally adjusted in the US and seasonally and calendar-adjusted in the euro area. Charted changes compare index levels. Public price measures use annual inflation rates. Changes from the crossing month are in percentage points and can reflect last year’s prices dropping out of the comparison. Household energy also includes electricity and gas, with different local weights, taxes and tariffs. US core excludes food and energy. Euro-area core also excludes alcohol and tobacco.

The euro-area series holds the current 21-country membership fixed across history. Eurostat flags earlier energy and core observations for a difference in historical definitions. In the 25% screen the March 2001 case has three missing euro-area inflation readings in its lead-in, September–November 2000. The source table shows the flags for each displayed observation. A missing source or horizon remains blank. Counts and medians use the available measurements.

Month-end benchmark policy rates come from the BIS series based on central-bank sources. For these events the US rate is the federal funds target or target-range midpoint, and the euro-area rate is the main refinancing rate. The 0.25% screen describes these observed rates. Monetary constraints also depend on expectations, asset purchases and the ECB deposit facility.
